questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following production possibility curves indicates increasing opportunity costs?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A production possibility curve (PPC) shows the maximum combinations of two goods that an economy can produce when all its resources are fully and efficiently used. Increasing opportunity cost means that each extra unit of one good costs more and more units of the other, because resources are not equally suited to both uses. The PPC is then bowed outwards from the origin, which the syllabus describes as a **concave** curve.

A straight-line PPC shows constant opportunity cost, and a PPC bowed inwards towards the origin (convex) would show decreasing opportunity cost. "Non-linear" is too vague, since a convex curve is also non-linear. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is the main reason for carrying out economic activity in a subsistence economy?
questions.corrige_markdown: In a subsistence economy households produce mainly for their own consumption, to satisfy their basic **needs** (food, shelter, clothing). There is little surplus, little trade and little specialisation, so production is not driven by preferences or by a wide range of wants. Choices are a consequence of scarcity, not the reason for producing. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A necessary condition for a mixed economy is that there are:
questions.corrige_markdown: A mixed economy combines the market mechanism with state intervention: resources are owned and allocated both by the **private sector** and by the **public sector**. Every economy has primary, secondary and tertiary activities, formal and informal activities, and capital and consumer goods, so none of these defines a mixed economy. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question is based on the items below:

i) Mineral deposits
ii) Plantations
iii) Lakes
iv) Grinding mills

From the above, land consists of:
questions.corrige_markdown: In economics "land" means all natural resources that are a free gift of nature: mineral deposits, lakes, forests, rivers, the sea and the soil. Plantations are planted and maintained by people (so they are capital) and grinding mills are manufactured capital goods. Land therefore consists of i (mineral deposits) and iii (lakes). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: For division of labour to be successfully implemented by a travel agency, the various related services need to be:
questions.corrige_markdown: Division of labour splits a job into separate tasks carried out by different workers or departments (ticketing, visas, hotel booking, transport). The customer receives one complete service only if the parts fit together, so the services must be **interdependent** and well co-ordinated. Efficiency and effectiveness are results of good organisation, not the condition that makes the division workable, and independent services would not combine into a single product. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question is based on the following items:

i. Shares are quoted in the stock exchange market
ii. Has limited liabilities
iii. Publishes annual balance sheet
iv. Possesses a trading certificate

The above characteristics apply to which of the following business units?
questions.corrige_markdown: Only a **public (limited) company** may offer its shares to the general public and have them quoted on the stock exchange. It enjoys limited liability, must publish its annual accounts (balance sheet) and, once it has raised its minimum capital, receives a certificate allowing it to start trading. A private company cannot sell shares to the public, a cooperative society is not quoted, and a limited partnership has at least one partner with unlimited liability. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question is based on figure 1 below.

![fig-1](gce-al-economics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

Which of the following movements illustrates forward vertical integration?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the figure firm A grows cocoa, firm D makes chocolate, firm B makes textiles, firm C makes plastic plates and firm E produces rubber. **Forward vertical integration** is when a firm takes over, or merges with, a firm at a **later stage of the same production chain**, closer to the consumer. Cocoa is the raw material of chocolate, so the move from firm A (cocoa) to firm D (chocolate) is forward integration.

A to B (textiles) has no link with cocoa, and neither has A to C: these would be conglomerate (diversifying) moves. E to A (rubber to cocoa) is also unrelated, and B to D joins two unrelated products. Moving from chocolate back to cocoa would be backward integration. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: From firm A to firm B.
From firm B to firm D.
From firm E to firm A.
From firm A to firm D.

questions.enonce_markdown: Given the total number of people and total output for an area over time, which of the following can such data help you to determine?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Dividing total output by the total population gives output per head (per capita income). If this is tracked over time, and prices are held constant, the change shows whether the average person has more goods and services available, that is a **change in the standard of living**.

The population total alone would show population growth, but it would not need output data. Migration cannot be separated from births and deaths using totals, and population structure (age and sex distribution) needs data by age group. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Positive checks according to the Malthusian population doctrine suggest that population can be controlled by:
questions.corrige_markdown: Malthus argued that population tends to grow faster than the food supply. Population is held back by two kinds of check. **Positive checks** raise the death rate: famine, disease, war and natural disasters. **Preventive checks** lower the birth rate through moral restraint: late marriage, chastity and celibacy (and, in modern terms, family planning). Of the options, only famine is a positive check. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following explains why a fall in price from 150 FCFA to 50 FCFA raises quantity demanded from 10 units to 20 units?
questions.corrige_markdown:
When the price of a good falls, it becomes cheaper relative to its substitutes, so consumers switch towards it: this is the **substitution effect**. (The lower price also raises real income, the income effect, which reinforces the extra purchase.) Together they explain the downward-sloping demand curve and the rise in quantity demanded from 10 to 20 units.

Crowding out is the fall in private investment caused by government borrowing, and diminishing marginal returns is a supply-side concept linked to production. Diminishing marginal rate of substitution describes the shape of an indifference curve, not the response of demand to a price change. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The demand for a good is said to be fairly inelastic if the value of its price elasticity is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Price elasticity of demand is the ratio of the percentage change in quantity demanded to the percentage change in price (taken in absolute value). Demand is fairly (relatively) inelastic when the value lies between 0 and 1: quantity responds less than proportionately to a price change. Of the options, only 0.2 is in that range.

A value of 0 means perfectly inelastic, 10 means fairly (very) elastic, and infinity means perfectly elastic. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question is based on figure 2 below.

![fig-2](gce-al-economics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

Why is the Sa portion of the above curve negatively-sloped?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The curve is an individual's supply curve of labour: the price axis is the wage rate and the quantity axis is the hours of work offered. Up to point a, a higher wage makes workers offer more hours. Beyond a, the curve bends backwards (the Sa portion): at a very high wage the worker can reach the desired income by working fewer hours, and the income effect outweighs the substitution effect, so the worker chooses to enjoy **more leisure** and works less.

So the negative slope reflects a **preference for leisure over work** at high wages, not a lack of affordability or profitability. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: More preference for work than leisure.
Price is too high to be afforded by all.
More preference for leisure than work.
High price makes supply very profitable.

questions.enonce_markdown: A situation in which price is reduced and total revenue instead falls, suggests that demand for the good is:
questions.corrige_markdown: Total revenue is price multiplied by quantity sold. If demand is elastic, a price cut raises quantity by a larger percentage than the fall in price, so revenue rises. If demand is unit elastic, revenue is unchanged. Revenue **falls** after a price cut only when the percentage rise in quantity is smaller than the percentage fall in price, that is when demand is **inelastic** (elasticity below 1). Of the options this is "fairly inelastic". **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that at the price of 8 FCFA, quantity demanded is 50 units and price elasticity of demand is 0.8. If price increases to 12 FCFA, what will be the change in quantity demanded?:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Use $E_d = \dfrac{\%\Delta Q_d}{\%\Delta P}$ in absolute value.

- Percentage change in price: $\dfrac{12-8}{8}\times 100 = 50\%$.
- Percentage change in quantity demanded: $0.8 \times 50\% = 40\%$, and it is a **fall** because price rises.
- Change in quantity: $\dfrac{40}{100}\times 50 = 20$ units.

Quantity demanded falls from 50 to 30 units, a change of **20 units**. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When the supply of an agricultural product is inelastic while its demand is fairly elastic, it will lead to:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The cobweb model describes price and output cycles in agriculture, where farmers decide output on last season's price. The type of cobweb depends on the relative elasticities. If **supply is less elastic than demand**, each price swing produces a smaller output response and the price fluctuations get smaller and smaller around the equilibrium: the cobweb is **convergent**. If supply is more elastic than demand the cobweb is divergent (exploding), and if both are equally elastic the fluctuations stay constant (a perfect or continuous cobweb).

Here supply is inelastic and demand is fairly elastic, so the cobweb converges. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Allocative and productive efficiency are easily achieved in the long run under a(an):
questions.corrige_markdown: In the long run a perfectly competitive firm produces where price equals marginal cost (allocative efficiency) and at the minimum point of its average cost curve (productive efficiency), because free entry and exit remove supernormal profit. A monopoly restricts output and charges a price above marginal cost, and monopolistic competition and oligopoly leave firms with excess capacity or price above marginal cost. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question is based on the following features of a firm:

- No advertising.
- Many buyers and sellers.
- No barriers to entry and exit.
- Profit maximization.

Identify the market structure that is best described by the above features.
questions.corrige_markdown: Many buyers and sellers, freedom of entry and exit and a homogeneous product (so no need for advertising) are the characteristics of **perfect competition**. Monopolistic competition has differentiated products and advertising, and oligopoly has a few large firms with barriers to entry. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question refers to figure 3 below which shows the demand curve for a firm in Oligopoly market.

![fig-3](gce-al-economics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

Price stability at OP indicates that there is :
questions.corrige_markdown: The figure shows the kinked demand curve of an oligopolist, with the kink at point G, price OP and output Oq. The curve is flatter (elastic) above G and steeper (inelastic) below G, because a firm expects rivals **not to follow a price rise** but **to follow a price cut**. A firm that raises its price loses many customers, and one that cuts its price gains little, so price stays at OP even when costs change. The firm keeps the price stable because it is **uncertain** how its rivals will react. Competition (including non-price competition such as advertising) continues, so the other options are wrong. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If TC exceeds TR by the least amount, it implies that the firm is:
questions.corrige_markdown: If total cost is greater than total revenue, the firm makes a loss equal to $TC - TR$. The output at which this gap is the **smallest** is the output at which the loss is as small as possible: the firm is **minimising its losses**. Maximising losses would mean the biggest gap, and normal profit occurs only when $TC = TR$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question is based on table 1 below which shows the output, costs, and revenue of a hypothetical firm.

*Table 1*

| Output | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Total Costs (FCFA) | 100 | 200 | 250 | 290 | 300 |
| Total Revenue | 0 | 175 | 350 | 525 | 700 |

From the table, it can be concluded that the firm is:
questions.corrige_markdown: Average revenue (price) is $TR \div Q$: $175 \div 1 = 175$, $350 \div 2 = 175$, $525 \div 3 = 175$ and $700 \div 4 = 175$. Price stays at **175 FCFA** whatever the output, and marginal revenue is also 175 FCFA each time ($TR$ rises by 175 per unit). A firm that can sell any quantity at a constant price is a price taker facing a horizontal demand curve, which is the case in **perfect competition**. A monopolist, a monopolistic competitor or an oligopolist faces a downward-sloping demand curve, so it would have to lower its price to sell more and total revenue would not rise in equal steps. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The main feature for firms to operate in the monopolistic market is:
questions.corrige_markdown: The market of monopolistic competition has many firms, free entry and exit, and, above all, **differentiated products** (branding, quality, packaging, location), which gives each firm some control over its price. Collusion and price rigidity are typical of oligopoly, and price discrimination is possible under monopoly. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The proportion of labour costs to total costs is a determinant of :
questions.corrige_markdown: According to Marshall's rules of derived demand, the demand for labour is more inelastic when labour costs are a **small proportion of total costs**: a wage rise then increases the firm's total cost only slightly, so the firm cuts back little on its workers. When labour cost is a large share of total cost, a wage rise raises costs a lot and the demand for labour is more elastic. The proportion of labour costs therefore determines the **elasticity of demand for labour**. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: elasticity of supply of a good.
elasticity of demand for a good.

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question is based on figure 4 below

![fig-4](gce-al-economics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

From the above figure, total earnings minus transfer earnings will result in the area indicated by letter:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the figure the equilibrium wage is OP and the number of workers employed is OQ.

- **Total earnings** of the workers = wage $\times$ workers = area under the line from P, that is Y + Z.
- **Transfer earnings** = what workers must be paid to keep them in this employment (the area under the supply curve) = Z.
- Total earnings minus transfer earnings = Y + Z - Z = **Y**, the area between the wage line and the supply curve. This surplus is **economic rent**.

X is the surplus of the employers (between the demand curve and the wage line), and W lies beyond the employment level OQ. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following theories explains the current rate of savings as the main determinant of the supply of loanable funds?
questions.corrige_markdown: The **classical (loanable funds) theory** says that the rate of interest is determined by the demand for loanable funds (mainly investment) and the supply of loanable funds, which comes from **current savings**, so the interest rate adjusts until saving equals investment. The Keynesian theory explains interest by liquidity preference (the demand for and supply of money), not by savings. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: One of the roles of profit in an economy is that:
questions.corrige_markdown: Profit is the reward of the entrepreneur, the factor of production that organises the other factors and bears the risk of production. Rewarding forgone liquidity and postponed consumption are roles of interest, the reward of capital. The option "it encourages invention and innovation" is a consequence of the profit motive, but the direct role of profit as a factor reward is the reward for entrepreneurship. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: it is a reward for entrepreneurship.
it is a compensation for postponing current consumption.

questions.enonce_markdown: Including only the values of final output in the calculation of national income helps to avoid:
questions.corrige_markdown: Intermediate goods (for example flour bought by a bakery) are already included in the price of the final goods (bread). If both were counted, the same output would be counted more than once. Counting **final output only** (or only the value added at each stage) avoids **double counting**. It does nothing about omissions, the black market or the hidden economy. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The loss in the value of capital assets over time refers to:
questions.corrige_markdown: Machines, buildings and vehicles wear out and become obsolete as they are used. This loss of value is called **capital consumption** (depreciation) and is deducted from GNP to obtain net national product. Capital appreciation is a rise in value, and capital deepening is an increase in capital per worker. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question relates to the formula below.

$$
\frac{\text{Base year price index}}{\text{Current year price index}} \times \frac{\text{National income}}{1}
$$

The formula above is used for calculating:
questions.corrige_markdown: National income measured at current prices (nominal national income) is **deflated** by multiplying it by the ratio of the base-year price index to the current-year price index. This removes the effect of price changes and gives **real national income**. For example, suppose the nominal national income is 1200 and the price index has risen from 100 to 120: real national income is $\frac{100}{120} \times 1200 = 1000$. No division by population appears in the formula, so it is not a per capita measure. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The value of all goods and services produced in an economy in a given period is known as:
questions.corrige_markdown: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total value of all final goods and services produced **within** the geographical boundaries of an economy in a year, whoever owns the factors of production. GNP adds net property income from abroad, NNP deducts capital consumption from GNP, and national income is the net total income earned by a country's residents. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question is based on figure 5 below.

![fig-5](gce-al-economics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

Autonomous dissaving is represented by the value
questions.corrige_markdown: In the figure S is the saving (withdrawal) function and I is the investment (injection) line. The saving curve cuts the vertical axis at point a, below the origin o. At zero income, saving is negative: households consume more than they earn and finance it from past savings or borrowing. This negative saving, which does not depend on income, is **autonomous dissaving**, measured by the distance **oa**. The distance bY1 is the level of saving (equal to investment) at equilibrium income Y1, and oc is the level of investment. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question is based on table 2 below showing a partial accelerator table for an economy with a capital-output ratio of 2:1. Depreciation is constant at a rate of 1000 units of capital per year.

*Table 2*

| Year | Demand | Existing capital | Required capital | Replacement investment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1000 | 2000 | 2000 | 1000 |
| 2 | 2000 | 2000 | 4000 | 1000 |
| 3 | 2500 | 4000 | 5000 | 1000 |
| 4 | 2500 | 5000 | 5000 | 1000 |
| 5 | 1500 | 5000 | 3000 | 00 |

What is the most appropriate reason why replacement investment in year 5 is zero?
questions.corrige_markdown:
With a capital-output ratio of 2:1, required capital is twice demand: in year 5, $2 \times 1500 = 3000$. Existing capital in year 5 is 5000, so the economy has **excess capacity** of $5000 - 3000 = 2000$ units of capital. Because the existing stock is already larger than the stock required, the firms do not need to replace the 1000 units that wear out each year, and replacement investment is zero.

Demand has fallen by 1000 (from 2500 to 1500) and required capital by 2000 (from 5000 to 3000), but these describe the change, not the reason why replacement is not needed. The excess capacity is 2000, not 1000. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Because required capital has fallen by 2000.

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question is based on the formula below:

$$
\frac{\text{Change in consumption}}{\text{Change in disposable income}}
$$

The formula above is used for calculating:
questions.corrige_markdown: The ratio $\dfrac{\Delta C}{\Delta Y_d}$ shows by how much consumption changes when disposable income changes by one unit. This is the **marginal propensity to consume** (MPC). The average propensity to consume is the ratio of total consumption to total income, $\dfrac{C}{Y}$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If C= 70Million FCFA + 0.7Y, where Y is income which of the following will stand for the saving function?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Income is either consumed or saved, so $S = Y - C$.

$$
S = Y - (70\text{ million} + 0.7Y) = -70\text{ million FCFA} + 0.3Y
$$

Autonomous consumption of 70 million FCFA gives negative saving of 70 million FCFA at zero income, and the marginal propensity to save is $1 - 0.7 = 0.3$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the income of an unskilled individual is 0 FCFA and his consumption is 1300 FCFA, what will this amount of consumption be referred to?
questions.corrige_markdown: Consumption that takes place even when income is zero does not depend on income. It is financed by past savings, borrowing or help from others. This is **autonomous consumption**, the constant term in the consumption function $C = a + bY$ (here $a = 1300$ FCFA). Induced consumption is the part that changes with income. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question is based on the following formula:

$$
\frac{1}{\text{MPS}}
$$

The formula above seeks to calculate
questions.corrige_markdown: The investment multiplier is $k = \dfrac{1}{1 - \text{MPC}} = \dfrac{1}{\text{MPS}}$ in a simple closed economy with no government. For example, if MPS is 0.25, the multiplier is 4, so a rise in investment of 100 million FCFA raises national income by 400 million FCFA. The accelerator is the ratio of induced investment to the change in output, and MPS itself is $\Delta S / \Delta Y$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question is based on table 3 below.

*Table 3*

| Year | Velocity of circulation of money | Price index |
|---|---|---|
| 2014 | 18 | 100 |
| 2015 | 12 | 95 |

It can be concluded that:

*Options as printed:* A) the standard of living has risen.   B) the rate of inflation has risen.   C) the cost of living has risen.   D) the value of money has fallen.
To which group of customers below will BICEC bank Cameroon issue certificates of deposit?
questions.corrige_markdown: A certificate of deposit is a document issued by a bank to a customer who deposits a sum of money for a fixed period at an agreed rate of interest. It is issued to **depositors**, not to borrowers, and since the funds are tied up for a fixed longer term (instead of being available on demand like a current or ordinary savings account), the group concerned is the **long term depositors**. The certificate may then be used or sold before maturity in some systems. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A hypothetical commercial bank keeps 20,000 FCFA after receiving 200,000 FCFA as deposit from a customer. The maximum additional deposit created is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The bank keeps 20,000 of the 200,000 FCFA as reserve, so the reserve ratio is $\dfrac{20\,000}{200\,000} = 10\%$. The credit (deposit) multiplier is $\dfrac{1}{0.10} = 10$.

- Maximum total deposits in the banking system: $200\,000 \times 10 = 2\,000\,000$ FCFA.
- This total includes the original deposit of 200,000 FCFA.
- Maximum **additional** deposits created = $2\,000\,000 - 200\,000 = 1\,800\,000$ FCFA.

The trap is option A, which is the total deposits including the original one. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question is based on the formula below:

$$
\frac{ED}{ES + ED} \times \text{Amount of tax}
$$

Where ED is the elasticity of demand and ES is the elasticity of supply.

The formula above best calculates the:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The burden of an indirect tax is shared between consumers and producers according to the elasticities. The more elastic demand is, the more easily consumers avoid the tax, so the burden falls on the producer. The producer's share is therefore proportional to the elasticity of **demand**:

$$
\text{Producer's share} = \frac{ED}{ES + ED} \times \text{tax}, \qquad \text{Consumer's share} = \frac{ES}{ES + ED} \times \text{tax}
$$

Check with an example: if $ED = 3$ and $ES = 1$, the producer pays $\frac{3}{4}$ of the tax and the consumer $\frac{1}{4}$. The two shares add up to the full tax. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question is based on table 5 below showing the tax structures in a number of countries.

*Table 5*

| Country | | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| | Income | 50,000 | 100,000 | 200,000 |
| X | Tax paid | 5000 | 10,000 | 20,000 |
| W | Tax paid | 10,000 | 20,000 | 25,000 |
| Y | Tax paid | 5,000 | 5,000 | 5,000 |
| Z | Tax paid | 5,000 | 15,000 | 40,000 |

In which of the above countries does the tax system respect the canon of vertical equity?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Vertical equity means that people with a greater ability to pay should pay a larger share of their income in tax, which is a **progressive** tax system. Compute tax as a percentage of income for incomes of 50,000, 100,000 and 200,000:

| Country | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3 | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| X | 10% | 10% | 10% | proportional |
| W | 20% | 20% | 12.5% | not progressive (falls at the highest income) |
| Y | 10% | 5% | 2.5% | regressive (fixed amount) |
| Z | 10% | 15% | 20% | progressive |

Only **country Z** has a tax rate that rises as income rises, so it is the only one that respects vertical equity. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: XYZ enterprise succeeds in transferring one quarter of its indirect tax to its customers. This implies that the demand for the product is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
If the customers bear only one quarter of the tax, then the producer bears three quarters. The consumer's share is $\dfrac{ES}{ES + ED} = \dfrac{1}{4}$, which gives $ED = 3 \times ES$: demand is more elastic than supply. When demand is elastic, consumers can reduce their purchases easily, so the firm cannot pass on much of the tax. Demand is therefore **fairly elastic**.

If demand were inelastic, the firm would pass on most of the tax, and if it were perfectly inelastic, all of it. If demand were perfectly elastic, none could be passed on, which does not agree with one quarter. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question is based on the list below:

i. Central government
ii. Local governments
iii. Public corporations
iv. Public Companies

The public sector consists of :
questions.corrige_markdown: The public sector is made up of the organisations owned and controlled by the state: central government, local governments (councils) and **public corporations** (state-owned enterprises, for example a national water or electricity corporation). Public companies (public limited companies) are owned by private shareholders and belong to the **private sector**, even though their shares are open to the public. So the public sector consists of i, ii and iii. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If countries have different opportunity cost ratios, and their international terms of trade (TOT) lie within limits set by their domestic opportunity cost ratios, the countries will find it:
questions.corrige_markdown: According to the theory of comparative advantage, trade is possible and **beneficial** when the countries' domestic opportunity cost ratios differ. For example, suppose that in country A one unit of cocoa costs 2 units of coffee at home and in country B it costs 4 units of coffee. If the terms of trade settle between 2 and 4 units of coffee per unit of cocoa, A obtains coffee more cheaply by exporting cocoa and B obtains cocoa more cheaply by exporting coffee. Both gain, so trade is **profitable** to both. **Answer: D.**

impossible to trade with each other.
profitable to trade with each other.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is an immediate and unavoidable result of devaluation other things being equal?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Devaluation lowers the external value of the currency. The price of exports in foreign currency falls, while the price of imports in the domestic currency rises. The terms of trade (export price index divided by import price index $\times 100$) therefore fall at once: this is an **unfavourable movement in the terms of trade**, and it is unavoidable.

The balance of trade does not improve immediately: because demand for exports and imports is inelastic in the short run (the J-curve), the trade balance often worsens first and improves later if the Marshall-Lerner condition is satisfied. So only the terms-of-trade effect is immediate and certain. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: An unfavourable movement in the terms of trade.
A favourable movement in the terms of trade.
A favourable movement in the balance of trade.
An unfavourable movement in the balance of trade.

questions.enonce_markdown: If short term measures fail to cure a country's balance of payments deficit, the best possible thing to do is to:
questions.corrige_markdown: Borrowing from abroad, using up foreign assets and raising interest rates (to attract short-term capital) are short-term ways of financing or reducing a deficit, and they do not solve its cause. If they fail, the lasting remedy is to correct the underlying imbalance, for example by **encouraging exports** (export promotion, diversification of exports, improving competitiveness and productivity), which raises foreign exchange earnings in the long term. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The J-curve effect explains that:
questions.corrige_markdown: After a devaluation, import prices rise at once, but the volumes of imports and exports adjust slowly because contracts, habits and supply take time to change. The demand for exports and imports is inelastic in the short run, so the import bill rises more than export earnings and the balance of payments gets **worse first**. Later the quantities adjust and, if the Marshall-Lerner condition is met, the balance **improves**. The path of the balance over time looks like the letter J. **Answer: C.**

revaluation improves BOP situation in the short run but worsens in the long run.
devaluation worsens BOP situation in the short run but improves in the long run.
devaluation improves BOP situation in the short run but worsens in the long run.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following statements is true?
questions.corrige_markdown: Economic growth is a sustained rise in real national output. Economic development is wider: it includes growth together with improvements in living standards, health, education and the structure of the economy. Growth is **necessary but not sufficient** for development, because a country needs more output to pay for better health, education and incomes, but growth can occur without development if the gains go to a small group. So development **cannot occur without growth**. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Economic development occurs without economic growth.
Economic growth occurs after economic development.
Economic development cannot occur without economic growth.
Economic development cannot co-exist with economic growth.

questions.enonce_markdown: Periodic fluctuations in economic activity most likely to reduce employment occur during a:
questions.corrige_markdown: In the trade (business) cycle, output and employment fall in the downswing and reach their lowest point in the slump (depression or trough), where firms cut production and lay off workers. Employment rises in recovery and boom, and is at its highest around the peak. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A country's labour force includes all those who are economically active. Economically active refers to those who are:
questions.corrige_markdown: The economically active population consists of people of working age who are **both willing and able to work**, whether they are employed or unemployed and looking for a job. Those who are able but not willing (for example full-time students, or people who have given up looking) and those unable to work (the sick, the disabled) are outside the labour force. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The removal of government regulation that restrict entry and exit of firms and competition is called:
questions.corrige_markdown: **Deregulation** is the removal of legal restrictions on entry into and exit from an industry, so that more firms can compete (for example, opening telecommunications or air transport to private operators). Denationalisation (privatisation) is a change of ownership from the state to private owners, leasing is renting out a state asset to a private operator, and contracting out is the hiring of private firms to supply a public service. **Answer: A.**
